cards.title: Lisbon
cards.sub: 11 cards · ~25 min · sit down knowing what you're doing

cards.title: Not tapas, however much they look like it
cards.body: Petiscos are ordered for the table and shared, but they don't come free with a drink and you don't eat them standing up: they're a whole meal made of small plates. And one of them changed the history of another cuisine: «peixinhos da horta» — green beans in batter, fried — travelled with Portuguese missionaries to sixteenth-century Japan. The Japanese changed the name. Today they call it tempura.

cards.question: You order «uma imperial» in a Lisbon bar. What arrives?
cards.explain: A small glass of draught beer, around 20 centilitres, very cold. It's the default measure: ask for «a beer» and this is what you get. In Porto the same thing is called a «fino», and calling it an imperial there is how you tell them where you're from.

cards.title: Two sandwiches and one rule
cards.body: The bifana is pork marinated in garlic and white wine, sliced thin, in a soft roll: the street sandwich. The prego is a beef steak in the same roll, and it comes with a rule nobody explains: in the cervejarias you order it at the end, after the seafood, the way you'd order dessert. Watching a whole table finish off the prawns with a prego is the most Lisbon scene there is.

cards.claim: «A pastel de nata is eaten cold, like a cake»
cards.body: It's eaten warm, fresh out, with the custard still trembling. Cold it's a different pastry — a worse one. And the cinnamon and icing sugar don't come on it: they're on the counter, in two shakers, and everyone adds their own. Lisboetas argue about this with the seriousness other people reserve for football.

cards.title: The night the whole city smells of sardines
cards.body: On 12 June Lisbon drags the grills out into the street. Whole sardines, ungutted, laid on a slice of bread that acts as the plate and soaks up the fat: you eat the bread last, and it's the best part. People give each other a «manjerico», a pot of basil with a paper carnation and a verse, and dance in the street until dawn. It's the city's biggest party, and it's in almost no guidebook.

cards.question: Portugal eats more fish than any other country in Europe. How many kilos per person a year?
cards.explain_correct: About 57 kilos per person per year, three times the European average and among the top three in the world. When someone here says «there's fish today», it isn't a suggestion: it's the norm.
cards.explain_wrong: About 57 kilos per person per year — three times the European average and among the top three in the world. Here «there's fish today» isn't a suggestion: it's the norm.

cards.title: If you see a sign saying «Há caracóis», go in
cards.body: From May to September, bars announce it on a handwritten sheet of paper. They're small snails, boiled with oregano and garlic, served in a deep plate with an imperial alongside. You pick them out with a toothpick, one by one, no hurry: it's a way to spend an afternoon, not a dish. It's wherever the Lisboetas are and missing wherever the tourists are.

cards.question: Someone recommends «a tasca» for lunch. What is it?
options: A neighbourhood tavern with a dish of the day
A tobacconist that also serves coffee
cards.explain: A small neighbourhood tavern, with the «prato do dia» written on a sheet of paper by the door and the house wine in a jug. You eat well, fast and cheap, at a shared table if need be. It's where people who work nearby eat, which is why by two o'clock there's no room left.

cards.title: Vinho verde isn't green
cards.body: It's young: «verde» means unaged, not the colour. It comes from the Minho, in the wet north, and it turns out light, sharp, with a natural touch of fizz no other wine has. You drink it very cold, with fish, and you order it without fear of looking wrong: everyone here drinks it. It's the summer wine of a country that barely exports it — which is why hardly anyone abroad knows it.

cards.question: You order «um galão» in a café. What arrives?
options: Coffee with lots of milk, in a tall glass
cards.explain: A tall glass, three-quarters milk and a quarter coffee: the Lisbon breakfast. «Meia de leite» is half and half, in a cup. «Abatanado» is a long black, and «pingado» an espresso with a drop of milk. Coffee here has more names than sizes, and knowing three of them changes the look on the waiter's face.

cards.title: The rice that has to be wet
cards.body: If you're coming from Spain, forget paella. Portuguese rice is called «malandro» — a rascal — when it's the way it should be: soupy, almost a broth, served in a pot and eaten with a spoon. Seafood rice, monkfish rice, roast duck rice. Dry rice here is rice done badly. It's the only rule, and it's the opposite of the one you brought with you.
